title: NASA's Swift Observatory Burns Up Over Indonesia After 22 Years in Orbit
excerpt: The 3,200-pound gamma-ray telescope re-entered at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra, ending a two-year mission that ran for nearly 22 years — months after a rescue spacecraft failed to save it.
body:
• NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory — 3,200 pounds (1,452 kg) — re-entered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday over Indonesia's North Sumatra province and burned up, with no damage or injuries reported.
  • The $500 million observatory launched on November 20, 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts and worked for nearly 22 years.
  • Swift had no propulsion of its own; increased solar activity puffed up the upper atmosphere and dragged it down, and a rescue spacecraft failed to boost its orbit less than three months ago.
  • NASA had put the risk of debris harming anyone on Earth at about 1 in 2,100.

NASA's Swift satellite telescope, which spent two decades studying the most powerful known blasts of energy in the cosmos, tumbled out of orbit on Wednesday and burned up in Earth's atmosphere over Indonesia, the space agency reported. The US Space Force confirmed the re-entry occurred at 7:39 a.m. EST, as the satellite streaked into the upper atmosphere at about 22 times the speed of sound over North Sumatra province, roughly 200 miles north of the equator, according to Reuters.

NASA said it expected the frictional heat of re-entry to incinerate most of the 3,200-pound observatory well above the surface, with some fragments possibly surviving the plunge. The agency reported no damage or injuries on the ground. It was not immediately clear how close the re-entry point was to Medan, North Sumatra's capital and largest city, home to about 2.5 million people. The Space Force had earlier calculated the odds of harm coming to anyone on Earth at one chance in 2,100, CNN reported.

A two-year mission that ran for 22

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory launched atop a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral on November 20, 2004, carrying a multi-wavelength array of three telescopes designed to catch gamma-ray bursts — the most intense blasts of energy in the universe — and study their afterglows. It was built for a two-year design life and outlasted it by two decades, becoming a general-purpose astrophysics tool with no direct replacement waiting.

Why it fell

Swift had no propulsion system of its own, so it could not fight atmospheric drag. Its demise was hastened by an increase in solar activity over the past couple of years, as the Sun reached the peak of its 11-year cycle in 2024 and puffed up Earth's upper atmosphere. The spacecraft eventually dropped to just 171 miles above the planet and could no longer compensate for the drag. It ceased operations on October 20, when researchers at Penn State — NASA's partner on the project and home to its Mission Operations Center — sent the final command. A rescue spacecraft sent to boost Swift to a higher orbit and extend its life failed its mission less than three months before the re-entry, a last attempt covered by the Times of India, which put the rescue effort's cost at $30 million.

What it leaves behind

Swift's archive — two decades of gamma-ray burst detections and rapid follow-up observations shared with telescopes worldwide — remains its scientific legacy. Its uncontrolled return is also a reminder of the limits of early-2000s satellite design: a flagship observatory with no thrusters was always going to end this way once solar activity picked up. Modern debris-mitigation standards, updated in 2019, require uncontrolled re-entries to carry an expected casualty risk below 1 in 10,000 — a bar Swift, designed before those standards, did not have to meet.
